solution_steps: Shares bought = 10 lots x 75 shares per lot = 750 shares.
Gain per share = exit premium - entry premium = 80 - 50 = Rs 30.
Gross gain = 750 x 30 = Rs 22,500.
Net profit = 22,500 - 225 (expenses) = Rs 22,275.

topic_name: Equivalent production — FIFO and weighted average
short_explanation: Equivalent units are the 6,600 units transferred out plus 600 equivalent units in closing WIP (1,000 x 60%); normal loss carries no equivalent units, giving 7,200.
explanation_text: Normal loss is an expected, unavoidable loss. It is assigned no cost and therefore no equivalent units; its cost is absorbed by the good output. Here input 8,000 = transferred 6,600 + normal loss 400 (5% of 8,000) + closing WIP 1,000, so the unit reconciliation balances exactly and there is no abnormal loss or gain to account for.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 6,200 units appears to net the normal loss out of the transferred units, which is wrong twice over.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 7,600 units treats closing WIP as fully complete (6,600 + 1,000).

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 6,800 units takes WIP at only 20% completion.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 6,300 units does not follow from any consistent treatment.

solution_steps: Input = 8,000 units; normal loss = 5% x 8,000 = 400 units.
Units accounted for: transferred 6,600 + normal loss 400 + closing WIP 1,000 = 8,000 (reconciles, so no abnormal loss).
Equivalent units of transferred output = 6,600 (100% complete).
Equivalent units in closing WIP = 1,000 x 60% = 600.
Normal loss contributes 0 equivalent units.
Total equivalent units = 6,600 + 600 = 7,200 units.
formula_used: Equivalent units = Units transferred out + (Closing WIP units x % completion); normal loss = nil equivalent units
common_traps: 7,600 is the trap for candidates who forget to apply the 60% completion factor to WIP.

key_note: The cycle is circular, so any rotation of Expansion - Recession - Trough - Recovery is an equally valid answer. Option (a) Expansion, Recession, Trough, Recovery; option (b) Recession, Trough, Recovery, Expansion; and option (d) Recovery, Expansion, Recession, Trough are all rotations of the same sequence and all internally correct. Only (c) and (e) are genuinely wrong. Without a stated starting point the question has three defensible answers. The item needs a fixed anchor (e.g. 'starting from the peak') to be single-keyed.

solution_steps: Budgeted total cost = Actual total cost - 18,000 = 3,00,000 - 18,000 = Rs 2,82,000.

Budgeted variable cost = 2,82,000 - 87,000 = Rs 1,95,000.

When money demand is interest-inelastic, a large rate change is needed and the curve is steep, approaching the vertical classical case.

topic_name: Depreciation — methods, change in estimate, commencement
short_explanation: Written-down value after five years is Rs 6,00,000, raised by Rs 1,20,000 to Rs 7,20,000, spread over the revised remaining life of eight years, giving Rs 90,000 for year six.
explanation_text: A change in the estimated useful life or in the carrying amount is a change in accounting ESTIMATE, applied prospectively. Prior years' depreciation is not restated; the revised carrying amount is simply written off over the revised remaining life.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 1,00,000 spreads 8,00,000 over eight years or otherwise mishandles the carrying amount.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 1,20,000 is the original annual charge (12,00,000 over ten years), ignoring both revisions.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 50,000 does not follow from any consistent step.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

solution_steps: Original annual depreciation = 12,00,000 / 10 = Rs 1,20,000.
Accumulated depreciation after 5 years = 5 x 1,20,000 = Rs 6,00,000.
Written-down value at end of year 5 = 12,00,000 - 6,00,000 = Rs 6,00,000.
Add the Rs 1,20,000 increase in value: revised carrying amount = Rs 7,20,000.
Revised remaining life = (10 - 5) + 3 = 8 years.
Depreciation for year 6 = 7,20,000 / 8 = Rs 90,000.
formula_used: Revised annual depreciation = (Revised carrying amount - Residual value) / Revised remaining useful life
common_traps: Rs 1,20,000 is the trap: it is the original charge, picked by candidates who ignore the revision entirely.

topic_name: Absorption vs marginal costing — profit reconciliation
short_explanation: Absorption cost per unit is 25 + 20 + 10 + (3,00,000 / 60,000 = 5) = Rs 60, so 10,000 units in stock are valued at Rs 6,00,000.
explanation_text: Absorption costing includes fixed MANUFACTURING overhead in product cost; administrative costs, fixed or variable, are period costs and never enter inventory valuation. That is why the Rs 5 variable administrative cost and the Rs 2,00,000 fixed administrative cost are excluded here.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

solution_steps: Fixed manufacturing overhead per unit = 3,00,000 / 60,000 units produced = Rs 5.
Absorption cost per unit = Direct material 25 + Direct labour 20 + Variable manufacturing overhead 10 + Fixed manufacturing overhead 5 = Rs 60.
Administrative costs (Rs 5 variable and Rs 2,00,000 fixed) are period costs and excluded.
Closing inventory = 10,000 units x Rs 60 = Rs 6,00,000.
formula_used: Absorption cost per unit = DM + DL + Variable manufacturing OH + (Fixed manufacturing OH / Units produced)
common_traps: Rs 4,50,000 is the marginal-costing valuation — the trap for candidates who forget to absorb fixed factory overhead.

short_explanation: Quick assets are 8,00,000 - 2,00,000 = Rs 6,00,000, which over current liabilities of Rs 4,80,000 gives a quick ratio of 1.25.

topic_name: Issue at premium; securities premium reserve
short_explanation: The premium is 10% of the Rs 10 face value, that is Re 1 per share, so 1,00,000 shares carry Rs 1,00,000 of securities premium.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 10,00,000 is the face value of the issue, which goes to share capital.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 1,10,000 does not follow from any step.

option_rationales.rationale: Rs 11,00,000 is the total issue proceeds (capital plus premium).

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 90,000 does not follow from any step.

solution_steps: Premium per share = 10% of Rs 10 = Re 1.
Total premium = 1,00,000 shares x Re 1 = Rs 1,00,000.
This amount is credited to the Securities Premium Reserve; the Rs 10,00,000 face value goes to Share Capital.
formula_used: Securities Premium = (Issue price - Face value) x Number of shares issued

topic_name: Double entry and rules of debit and credit

topic_name: Standard costing — types of standards and ideal standard
short_explanation: Costs established in advance of production, against which actual costs are compared, are pre-determined (standard) costs.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Actual costs are ascertained after production.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Estimated costs are a looser forecast used for quotations; standard costing uses scientifically set pre-determined costs.

option_rationales.label: d

topic_name: Process costing — normal loss, abnormal loss, abnormal gain
short_explanation: Normal loss is 30% of 300 = 90 units, so expected output is 210; actual output of 190 falls short by 20, which is an abnormal loss of 20 units.
explanation_text: Abnormal loss is valued at the same rate as good output (after absorbing normal loss cost) and transferred to the Costing Profit and Loss Account, so it never distorts the cost of good production. Abnormal gain, the mirror case where actual output exceeds expected, is credited there.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: An abnormal gain would require output above the expected 210 units.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Output of 190 differs from the expected 210, so there is an abnormal item.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 30 units is the normal loss PERCENTAGE figure misread as units.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The shortfall is 20 units, not 30; 90 units is the normal loss.

solution_steps: Normal loss = 30% x 300 = 90 units.
Expected (normal) output = 300 - 90 = 210 units.
Actual output = 190 units.
Shortfall = 210 - 190 = 20 units, which is abnormal loss.
formula_used: Abnormal loss = Expected output (Input - Normal loss) - Actual output
common_traps: Computing 300 - 190 = 110 and calling the excess over normal loss 'abnormal' in the wrong direction is the usual error.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Low inflation with low unemployment is a benign outcome.

option_rationales.label: b

topic_name: Marginal costing — contribution and P/V ratio
short_explanation: At the break-even point contribution equals fixed cost, so P/V ratio = Fixed cost / BEP sales = 5 / 20 = 25%.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 15% does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 20% is the ratio of BEP to something else, not fixed cost to BEP sales.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 30% does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 35% does not follow from the figures.

solution_steps: At BEP, total contribution = fixed cost = Rs 5 lakhs.
BEP sales = Rs 20 lakhs.
P/V ratio = Contribution / Sales = 5 / 20 = 0.25 = 25%.
formula_used: BEP (value) = Fixed Cost / P/V Ratio, therefore P/V Ratio = Fixed Cost / BEP (value)
common_traps: Candidates invert the relation and compute 20/5, which gives a meaningless 400%.

short_explanation: 2,00,000 shares at Rs 12 (face Rs 10 plus 20% premium) brings in Rs 24,00,000, split Rs 20,00,000 to share capital and Rs 4,00,000 to securities premium.

option_rationales.label: b

topic_name: Calls in advance and calls in arrears

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Capital reserve arises from capital profits, not from early receipt of calls.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Securities premium is the excess over face value, a different item.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Share application money is received at the application stage, before allotment, not in advance of a later call.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Calls in arrear is the OPPOSITE — amounts called but not received.

common_traps: 'Calls in Arrear' is the mirror trap and sits at the end of the list where a hurried candidate lands.

topic_name: Format of financial statements governed by Schedule III
short_explanation: Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 prescribes the format of the balance sheet and statement of profit and loss.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The RBI Act prescribes formats for banks through the Banking Regulation Act, not for companies generally.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The Income-tax Act governs computation of taxable income.

common_traps: 'Accounting standards only' is the strong distractor; standards and Schedule III work together but the format is Schedule III's.

topic_name: Kurt Lewin styles — autocratic, democratic, laissez-faire
short_explanation: A manager who only instructs and ignores input is autocratic; one who seeks and weighs suggestions before deciding is democratic (participative).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Reverses the two managers.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Laissez-faire means leaving the team to itself, which neither manager does.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Neither manager is described as rule-bound or hands-off.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Neither is described in terms of vision or contingent reward.

common_traps: Democratic leadership still ends in the leader deciding — candidates sometimes call that autocratic.

topic_name: Law of demand and exceptional demand
short_explanation: The demand curve slopes downward from left to right because of the inverse price-quantity relation, and in exceptional cases (Giffen and Veblen goods) it slopes upward from left to right.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Downward right to left' misdescribes the standard orientation of the curve.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Calls the relationship direct, which contradicts the law of demand.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Misdescribes the standard slope orientation.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both misdescribes the orientation and calls the relationship direct.

common_traps: The item is really testing whether the candidate reads the direction phrase carefully; the economics is elementary.

topic_name: Margin of safety and angle of incidence
short_explanation: Margin of safety in value = Profit / P/V ratio = 12,000 / 0.3 = Rs 40,000.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 48,000 does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 8,400 does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 36,000 does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 24,000 does not follow from the figures.

Therefore Margin of safety = Profit / P/V ratio.

short_explanation: Section 144 prohibits all four — accounting and book-keeping, internal audit, investment advisory and management services — along with actuarial services, design of financial information systems, investment banking and outsourced financial services.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Omits investment advisory and management services, both prohibited.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: c

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Omits internal audit, which is prohibited.

short_explanation: With a currency-deposit ratio of 500/1100 and reserves of 12% plus excess reserves of 2 billion, the multiplier is (500 + 1100) / (500 + 132 + 2), which is about 2.52 — the nearest option.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 1.95 does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 2.20 does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 3.10 does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 4.00 does not follow from the figures.

solution_steps: Required reserves = 12% x 1,100 = Rs 132 billion; excess reserves = Rs 2 billion.
High-powered money (H) = Currency 500 + Total reserves (132 + 2) = Rs 634 billion.
Money supply (M) = Currency 500 + Demand deposits 1,100 = Rs 1,600 billion.
Money multiplier = M / H = 1,600 / 634 = 2.52.
formula_used: Money multiplier = (C + D) / (C + R) = (1 + c) / (c + r + e)
common_traps: Using 1/CRR alone gives 8.33 and ignores currency leakage, which is the dominant term here.
key_note: The exact computation gives 2.52, while the keyed option reads 2.54 — a small rounding discrepancy in the key. No other option is close, so the key is accepted; the option text should ideally be corrected to 2.52.

topic_name: AS 10 — property, plant and equipment; revaluation
short_explanation: Advertising and promotional costs for launching a product are period expenses and are expressly excluded from the cost of property, plant and equipment.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Installation and assembly costs are directly attributable and capitalised.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Site preparation is directly attributable and capitalised.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Professional fees for installation are directly attributable and capitalised.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Initial delivery and handling costs are directly attributable and capitalised.

common_traps: The standard lists advertising, staff training, and costs of opening a new facility as express exclusions — the item tests exactly that list.

topic_name: GST — supply, input tax credit, zero-rated, exports
short_explanation: The second proviso to section 16(2) of the CGST Act requires payment to the supplier within 180 days of the invoice date, failing which the credit availed is added to output tax liability with interest.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 90 days is not the prescribed period.

option_rationales.label: b

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: 150 days is not the prescribed period.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 365 days is not the prescribed period.

topic_name: Depreciation — methods, change in estimate, commencement
short_explanation: Depreciation begins when the asset is available for use — in the location and condition necessary for it to operate as management intends — not when it is bought or first used.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Purchase alone does not start depreciation if the asset is not yet ready for use.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Payment terms are irrelevant to depreciation.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Insurance is irrelevant to depreciation.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Installation is usually the last step before availability, but the trigger is availability for use, not the physical act of installation.

common_traps: 'Installed' is the sharpest distractor because installation is normally what makes an asset available; the standard's wording is availability for use.

short_explanation: A basic savings account meets the elementary need to hold money (physiological), a premium credit card confers status (esteem), insurance provides security (safety), and a personal relationship manager provides belonging and personal connection (social).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Places BSBDA at safety and insurance at physiological, reversing two of the four.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Places the premium card at social and the relationship manager at esteem, swapping the pair.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Misplaces all four.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Misplaces all four.

common_traps: The premium credit card and the relationship manager are the pair most easily swapped; status versus belonging is the discriminator.
key_note: The mapping of a basic savings account to physiological needs is a stretch — money is not itself a physiological need — but the option set offers no better consistent ordering, and the intended mapping is clear.

short_explanation: Fayol treated coordination as the function of harmonising and unifying all activities so that the organisation works as one.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Planning looks ahead and sets the course of action.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Organising arranges resources and structure.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Controlling checks performance against plan.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Staffing fills positions with people.

common_traps: Later writers treat coordination as the ESSENCE of management running through all functions rather than a separate one, which is why some texts list five functions and others six.

topic_name: Cost concepts — prime, production, conversion cost
short_explanation: Conversion cost is what it takes to convert raw material into finished output — direct labour plus production overhead — which equals cost of production less direct material.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Subtracting direct labour as well removes part of the conversion cost itself.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Subtracting production overheads too leaves nothing of the conversion cost.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Subtracting direct expenses as well understates conversion cost where direct expenses are part of converting material into output.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

formula_used: Conversion Cost = Direct Labour + Production Overheads = Cost of Production - Direct Material
common_traps: Option b is the trap for candidates who remember that conversion cost excludes material and over-apply the subtraction to labour as well.
key_note: Option (d) is arguably defensible under the stricter reading where direct expenses are listed separately from labour and overhead, since some texts define conversion cost as labour plus overhead only. The keyed option states the standard textbook identity.

topic_name: Indian fiscal year and budget calendar
short_explanation: The insurance FDI limit was proposed to rise from 74% to 100% for insurers investing the entire premium in India, NaBFID was to set up the Partial Credit Enhancement Facility for infrastructure corporate bonds, and an Investment Friendliness Index of States was announced.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The 51% to 74% step is the earlier 2021 change, and the RBI does not run the credit enhancement facility for infrastructure bonds.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Gets NaBFID right but uses the superseded FDI step and the wrong index name.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: SIDBI serves MSMEs, not infrastructure bond credit enhancement.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Gets the FDI step right but assigns the facility to the RBI and misnames the index.

common_traps: 51% to 74% is the designed trap: it was the real previous change and reads as familiar.

short_explanation: Cost reduction is corrective — it attacks the cost standard itself and continues to operate even where cost control is already working well.
explanation_text: Cost control is preventive and works towards a pre-set standard; once the standard is met, control has done its job. Cost reduction assumes no standard is final and permanently questions whether the same result can be achieved at lower cost, without sacrificing quality or utility.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Selective' describes scope, not the nature of the function.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Preventive is cost CONTROL's character, not cost reduction's.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Extensive' describes scope, not the nature of the function.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Detective' is an internal-control classification, not a cost-reduction descriptor.

common_traps: 'Preventive' is the designed trap because it is the correct adjective for the paired concept, cost control.

topic_name: Transfer to the Unpaid Dividend Account
short_explanation: Section 124(1) gives thirty days for payment and then seven days to transfer unpaid or unclaimed dividend to the Unpaid Dividend Account.
explanation_text: The Unpaid Dividend Account is only the first stage. Amounts that remain unclaimed in it for seven years, together with the underlying shares, are transferred to the Investor Education and Protection Fund under sections 124(5) and 124(6).

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: The payment window is thirty days, not fifteen, and the first transfer is to the Unpaid Dividend Account, not the IEPF.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: There is no 'Dividend Reserve Account' in section 124 and the period is seven days, not ten.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The payment window is thirty days and the first transfer is not to the IEPF.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: A dividend equalisation reserve is a voluntary accounting reserve, not the statutory destination.

common_traps: The IEPF options are the designed trap: the IEPF is the eventual destination, but only after seven years in the Unpaid Dividend Account.

topic_name: Waste, scrap, spoilage and defectives — treatment
short_explanation: Spoilage arising from inefficiency and capable of being controlled is abnormal spoilage; its cost is written off to the Costing Profit and Loss Account rather than absorbed by good output.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 'Ordinary spoilage' is not a standard classification.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 'Operational spoilage' is not a standard classification.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Normal spoilage is the unavoidable, expected loss inherent in the process; its cost IS borne by good output.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Defectives are units that can be rectified and sold as seconds; they are a different category from spoilage.

common_traps: 'Normal Spoilage' is the direct trap; the discriminator is controllability, and controllable means abnormal.

topic_name: Board composition — minimum and maximum directors
short_explanation: Section 149(1) requires a minimum of three directors for a public company, two for a private company, one for an OPC, with a maximum of fifteen.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Five is not the public company minimum.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Two, not three, is the private company minimum.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Both the public minimum and the maximum are wrong.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: The maximum is fifteen, not eleven; more than fifteen requires a special resolution.

common_traps: Seven is the minimum number of MEMBERS for a public company and is often confused with the minimum number of directors.

short_explanation: AS 2 excludes abnormal wastage from the cost of inventory; it is recognised as an expense of the period in which it is incurred.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Abnormal loss is not an asset — no future benefit flows from it.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Including it in inventory cost would carry a loss forward in the balance sheet, which is exactly what AS 2 forbids.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Deferral is not permitted.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Capitalising an abnormal loss is not permitted.

common_traps: Normal wastage IS absorbed in inventory cost, which is what makes the abnormal case examinable.

topic_name: GDP, GNP, NNP and NDP concepts
short_explanation: GDP is domestic-territory output (c), NNP at market price is residents' output net of depreciation at market prices (a), the GDP deflator is the price index (d), and disposable personal income is post-tax income available for consumption and saving (b).

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Assigns the NNP definition to GDP and the GDP definition to NNP.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Assigns the disposable income definition to GDP.

option_rationales.rationale: Assigns the deflator definition to GDP.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Uses definition b twice and leaves one definition unmatched.

common_traps: The GDP and NNP definitions are adjacent and the swap in option b is the designed trap.

topic_name: Vroom expectancy theory — valence, instrumentality, expectancy
short_explanation: Instrumentality is the belief that performing well will actually lead to the promised reward.
explanation_text: Vroom's model is Motivation = Expectancy x Instrumentality x Valence. Expectancy links effort to performance, instrumentality links performance to outcome, and valence is the value the individual places on the outcome. Because the terms multiply, a zero on any one collapses motivation to zero.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Effort leading to performance is EXPECTANCY.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: The value of the reward is VALENCE.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: The level of motivation is the product of all three, not one component.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Task difficulty affects expectancy but is not itself a component.

formula_used: Motivation = Expectancy x Instrumentality x Valence
common_traps: Expectancy and instrumentality are routinely swapped; the anchor is that instrumentality is the middle link.

short_explanation: The SEBI AIF Regulations cap an angel fund's investment in a single investee company at Rs 25 crore, raised from the earlier Rs 10 crore.

option_rationales.rationale: Rs 15 crore is not a prescribed ceiling.

option_rationales.rationale: Rs 20 crore is not a prescribed ceiling.

option_rationales.label: e

short_explanation: AS 10 covers ordinary plant and machinery and bearer plants, but excludes the produce growing on bearer plants and mineral rights such as mining rights.

option_rationales.rationale: Omits normal plant and machinery, which is squarely within AS 10.

option_rationales.rationale: Includes mining rights, which AS 10 expressly excludes.

option_rationales.rationale: Mining rights alone is the express exclusion, not the inclusion.

short_explanation: Statements 1, 2 and 4 are correct; statement 3 is wrong because for an inferior good the income demand curve slopes DOWNWARD — demand falls as income rises.

option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 4, which is correct.

option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is wrong.

option_rationales.rationale: Includes statement 3, which is wrong.

option_rationales.label: b

short_explanation: ABC analysis applies the Pareto 80-20 principle: a small proportion of items accounts for the bulk of inventory value and receives the tightest control.

short_explanation: Nadler defined HRD as comprising training, education and development; performance appraisal is a human resource management activity outside that triad.

short_explanation: All three statements describe forwards, futures and the basis correctly as intended: customised OTC forwards, standardised exchange-traded margined futures, and the spot-to-futures gap called the basis.

option_rationales.rationale: Omits statement 3, which the key treats as correct.

short_explanation: Section 52(2) permits the securities premium account to be applied to issuing fully paid bonus shares, writing off preliminary expenses or issue expenses, providing the premium on redemption of redeemable preference shares or debentures, and buy-back under section 68.

option_rationales.rationale: The securities premium is a capital reserve and cannot be distributed as dividend.

option_rationales.rationale: It cannot be used for routine operating expenses.

topic_name: Marginal costing — contribution and P/V ratio
short_explanation: Contribution is sales less variable cost — the amount available to cover fixed cost and then produce profit.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Fixed cost less profit is not a defined measure.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Sales less fixed cost is not contribution; contribution is computed before fixed cost.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Variable cost less fixed cost is meaningless.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Filler option; a correct answer is present.

short_explanation: Holding currency earns nothing, so its opportunity cost is the interest that could have been earned on an interest-bearing asset.

option_rationales.rationale: Inflation erodes real value but is a loss of purchasing power, not the forgone-alternative cost economists mean by opportunity cost of money balances.

topic_name: Katz's managerial skills — technical, human, conceptual
short_explanation: Katz held that technical skill matters most at the supervisory level, where the manager directs the actual work being done.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Conceptual skill is most important at top management.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Human skill is important at ALL levels roughly equally, so it does not distinguish the front line.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 'Strategic skill' is not one of Katz's three.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 'Political skill' is not one of Katz's three.

common_traps: Human skill is the tempting answer because supervisors deal with people constantly; Katz's point is that human skill is level-neutral.

topic_name: Real vs nominal income; GDP deflator
short_explanation: Nominal GDP = Real GDP x Price index / 100 = 1200 x 110 / 100 = 1320.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: 1200 is the real GDP itself, unadjusted.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: 1300 does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: 1400 does not follow from the figures.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: 1100 is the price index misread as an output figure.

Therefore Nominal GDP = Real GDP x Deflator / 100.
formula_used: Nominal GDP = Real GDP x (Price Index / 100)
common_traps: Dividing instead of multiplying gives 1,090.9, which is not offered; 1200 catches those who skip the adjustment entirely.

short_explanation: Insurance companies are required to present the cash flow statement using the direct method.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: The indirect method is the common choice for other enterprises but is not what insurers must use.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Only one method is prescribed for insurers.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Fund flow is a different statement altogether.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Accrual is a basis of accounting, not a cash flow presentation method.

short_explanation: Followers who are able but unwilling or insecure (readiness level R3) call for the participating style — high relationship, low task — where the leader shares ideas and supports rather than directs.
explanation_text: Hersey and Blanchard map four readiness levels to four styles: R1 (unable and unwilling) to Telling, R2 (unable but willing) to Selling, R3 (able but unwilling) to Participating, and R4 (able and willing) to Delegating.

option_rationales.label: a
option_rationales.rationale: Telling suits followers who are neither able nor willing.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Selling suits followers who are unable but willing.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Delegating suits followers who are both able and willing.

option_rationales.label: e

short_explanation: With no income or carrying cost, F = S(1 + rt), so S = 432 / (1 + 0.09 x 0.5) = 432 / 1.045 = about Rs 414.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Rs 425 would give a forward of about Rs 444.10.

solution_steps: Cost-of-carry relation with simple interest: Forward = Spot x (1 + r x t).
Interest factor for 6 months at 9% p.a. = 1 + (0.09 x 6/12) = 1.045.
Spot = Forward / 1.045 = 432 / 1.045 = Rs 413.4, which rounds to Rs 414.
formula_used: Forward Price = Spot Price x (1 + r x t), where r is the annual rate and t the time in years
common_traps: Deducting 9% of 432 for half a year (432 - 19.44 = 412.56) gives option b — a subtraction where a division is required.

topic_name: Certificates of deposit — denomination and maturity
short_explanation: Umbrella Ltd breaches three RBI norms at once: CDs must be in denominations of Rs 5 lakh and multiples thereof, must carry a minimum maturity of seven days, and no loan may be granted against a CD.
explanation_text: The RBI's Certificate of Deposit directions fix a minimum issue size of Rs 5 lakh with multiples of Rs 5 lakh thereafter, a maturity band of seven days to one year for CDs issued by banks (up to three years for select financial institutions), free transferability by endorsement and delivery, and a prohibition on the issuing bank granting loans against its own CDs or buying them back before maturity except as specifically permitted. Raincoat Ltd's practices — Rs 5 lakh multiples, six-month maturity, no loans against CDs, free transferability — comply on every count.

option_rationales.label: b
option_rationales.rationale: Raincoat's Rs 5 lakh multiples are exactly what the norms require, so there is no denomination breach.

option_rationales.label: c
option_rationales.rationale: Umbrella's CDs are freely transferable, which complies; its breaches lie elsewhere.

option_rationales.label: d
option_rationales.rationale: Raincoat's six-month maturity sits comfortably inside the seven-day to one-year band.

option_rationales.label: e
option_rationales.rationale: Umbrella breaches three norms, so it is not the case that both comply.

common_traps: Raincoat looks like the outlier because its terms are more restrictive than Umbrella's; restrictive practice within the permitted band is not a breach.
